name: Fondazione Pino Pascali
subtitle: Contemporary art in a former municipal slaughterhouse by the Adriatic
description: Plan a visit to Fondazione Pino Pascali in Polignano a Mare: contemporary art, official opening hours, admission, walking connections and practical advice.
intro: Polignano is more than a coastline to photograph. Fondazione Pino Pascali offers a different way to explore the town, through contemporary art and the work of an artist with family roots in Polignano a Mare. Its restored former municipal slaughterhouse brings cultural life into an industrial building. Make this a deliberate museum stop, with time for the exhibitions, rather than assuming every room contains a permanent Pascali display.
advice: Read the current exhibition programme before choosing your day; installations and works on view can change.
Allow around 60–90 minutes as an editorial planning estimate, adjusting for the exhibition and your interests.
Ask the museum about step-free access and any particular assistance you need before travelling.
highlights: An institution devoted to Pascali and contemporary artistic research.
A former municipal slaughterhouse adapted for cultural use.
A useful indoor cultural stop to combine with a walk through Polignano.
about: The institution began in 1998 with works and personal items donated by Pascali’s family and became a foundation in 2010. The current museum occupies the restored former municipal slaughterhouse. Its identity joins research into Pascali’s work with contemporary exhibitions. This history explains its significance, but does not mean that a particular artwork, room or exhibition will always be available during your visit.
hours: Checked 10 November 2026: the foundation lists Wednesday–Sunday, 10:00–13:00 and 16:00–20:00, with last admission at 12:30 and 19:30. Check its current contact page for holidays, installation periods or exceptional closures before setting out.
prices: Checked 10 November 2026: full admission €10; reduced admission €6 for visitors over 65 and Polignano residents. Under-18s and certain other categories enter free; the first Sunday of each month is free. Check eligibility and current conditions directly with the foundation.
transport: Regional trains on the Bari–Lecce line serve Polignano a Mare. Use Trenitalia for the timetable and fare for your travel date.
From the station or historic centre, use a walking route to Via Parco del Lauro 119; allow extra time for coastal stops.
If arriving by car, check local parking signs and access restrictions. Do not assume museum admission includes parking.

Reach Via Parco del Lauro and check admission and photography rules.
Follow the exhibition sequence and labels through the open galleries.

name: Cala Paura
subtitle: White pebbles, rocky edges and a coastal pause close to town
description: Explore Cala Paura in Polignano a Mare with practical advice on its pebble coves, public access, weather, walking routes and responsible photography.
intro: Cala Paura offers a smaller-scale coastal stop alongside Polignano’s better-known viewpoints. The regional tourism description highlights white pebbles enclosed by rocky sides, while municipal planning describes two small coves with both serviced and free areas. Come for the shape of the shoreline and a slow seaside pause. A visit does not have to include swimming, especially when wind or waves make the water unsuitable.
advice: Wear footwear suited to pebbles and slippery surfaces; this is not a flat promenade.
Check weather and on-site warnings; leave swimming out of the plan in rough conditions.
Allow roughly 30–60 minutes for a scenic stop as an editorial estimate, longer for an extended rest.
highlights: A white-pebble shoreline framed by rock.
Two small coves described in the municipal planning material.
A coastal stop that can be combined with the Modugno area and the historic centre.
about: Cala Paura belongs to the varied rocky coastline of Polignano a Mare. Official regional tourism material identifies its pebble beach, and the municipality distinguishes free areas from areas with services. These descriptions establish the setting, not the availability of every facility on a particular day. Treat beach services, rescue cover and access conditions as things to check locally rather than permanent guarantees.
hours: Checked 10 November 2026: no fixed public-shoreline visiting timetable was verified. Weather, maintenance or local restrictions may affect access. Check signs on arrival; daylight makes the terrain easier to assess.
prices: Checked 10 November 2026: the public beach area is free, while equipment hire, services and parking may cost extra. Municipal material distinguishes free and serviced areas; confirm charges with individual operators.
transport: Regional trains on the Bari–Lecce line serve Polignano a Mare. Check Trenitalia for current services and tickets.
From the historic centre or Modugno area, follow a mapped walking route and designated pedestrian access.
Check parking signs and seasonal restrictions. Do not drive onto beach access paths.

charm.title: The texture of the shore

charm.title: A pair of small coves
charm.text: The municipal description of two coves helps explain why services and access can differ within a compact area. Look at the signs for the part you intend to use.

charm.title: A quieter kind of itinerary
charm.text: A short shore visit works well between town walks. Treat a rest by the water as optional and let the conditions, rather than a rigid schedule, decide how long you stay.

Walk from the Modugno area to the mapped Cala Paura access.
Assess surfaces and warnings before choosing a safe stopping place.
Return towards the town, perhaps continuing to Arco Marchesale.

Take litter away and verify toilets, equipment hire and accessible routes locally if these are essential to your visit.

name: Arco Marchesale · Porta Grande
subtitle: The historic gateway between modern Polignano and its old town
description: Visit Arco Marchesale, also called Porta Grande: Polignano’s historic gateway, architectural details, free public passage and an old-town walking route.
intro: Arco Marchesale makes a natural introduction to Polignano’s historic centre. Also known as Porta Grande, it stands at the transition from the Piazza Garibaldi area into the old town. Rather than treating it only as a doorway to hurry through, pause to notice its defensive details. Then continue on foot towards Santa Maria Assunta and the small streets beyond, leaving room for everyday pedestrian traffic.
advice: Look at the gateway from both sides, but step out of the pedestrian flow before stopping.
Allow about 15–25 minutes as an editorial estimate for the exterior and architectural details.
Combine the gate with Santa Maria Assunta instead of planning it as a separate transport journey.
highlights: The old town’s historic main entrance, also called Porta Grande.
Traces of the former drawbridge mechanism in the gate structure.
A direct link between Piazza Garibaldi and the historic-centre walk.
about: The regional heritage catalogue relates the gateway to alterations to the fortifications around 1530. Until 1780 it was the old town’s only connection with the outside. Surviving details include holes associated with the drawbridge chains, defensive features and a small chapel above. These layers belong to the town’s evolving fortified entrance; they should not be mistaken for evidence that this is a surviving Roman gate.

charm.title: From defences to daily life

name: Chiesa Matrice di Santa Maria Assunta
subtitle: Polignano’s mother church and former cathedral in the heart of the old town
description: Discover Santa Maria Assunta in Polignano a Mare: its historic interior, parish access information, visitor etiquette and a walking route from Porta Grande.
intro: Santa Maria Assunta gives an old-town walk a place to slow down and look closely. On Piazza Vittorio Emanuele, Polignano’s mother church is both a historic monument and a living place of worship. If the church is open to visitors, its interior rewards a quiet, attentive visit. If services or local arrangements prevent entry, enjoy the square and exterior without treating access as guaranteed.
advice: Check with the parish before planning a visit around interior access; a general map listing is not a confirmed visiting timetable.
Allow around 20–40 minutes as an editorial estimate when sightseeing is permitted, with more time for an unhurried square visit.
Dress appropriately for a church and give worshippers priority over photography or sightseeing.
highlights: Polignano’s mother church and former cathedral.
A three-aisled interior with historic furnishings.
A stone Nativity by Stefano da Putignano, highlighted by regional cultural information.
about: The Puglia regional cultural account traces construction of the present church to 1295. It describes three aisles, an eighteenth-century high altar, a wooden choir, the chapel of San Vito and Stefano da Putignano’s stone Nativity. As the former cathedral and current mother church, the building connects the town’s religious history with parish life. Individual areas or artworks may not be accessible during every visit.
